title: Maitreyi's question
hookLine: a husband offers to split the estate before he leaves, and his wife asks the question that isn't about money
carry: atman: all we love, we love for the self
tomorrow: karma: what drives us, and the week looks back
last: THE UNIVERSE FITS IN HIS MOUTH.

cards: A well-known teacher named Yajnavalkya has decided to leave home. He has two wives, Katyayani and Maitreyi, and before he goes he wants to settle what he owns.
So he says to Maitreyi: let me make a settlement between you and Katyayani. It's a kind offer, and a practical one. Maitreyi could ask how much.
She asks something else entirely, and the Upanishad keeps her question, and the whole conversation it starts.

teach.b: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the great forest teaching. Maitreyi says: if this whole earth, filled with wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? Yajnavalkya, to his credit, is honest.
No. Your life would be like the life of rich people.

teach.h: NO HOPE OF IT THROUGH WEALTH.
teach.b: There's no hope of immortality through wealth. So she says: then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know.
He's delighted. You've always been dear to me, he says, and now you ask what's dearest. Then he teaches her.

teach.h: ALL IS DEAR FOR THE SAKE OF THE SELF.
teach.b: A husband is dear not for the husband's own sake, but for the sake of the Self. A wife is dear not for her own sake, but for the Self.

teach.h: HEAR IT, THINK IT, REST IN IT.
teach.b: Children, wealth, the whole world: all dear for the sake of the Self, the atman. Then the well-known line: the Self is what should be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on.
Later Vedanta teachers turned those words into a method in three steps: hearing the teaching, thinking it through, and resting in it until it's lived. That's still the backbone of the jnana road.

teach.h: ĀTMĀ VĀ ARE DRAṢṬAVYAḤ ŚROTAVYO MANTAVYO NIDIDHYĀSITAVYAḤ.
teach.b: Not in a monastery. At a moment of loss, a family changing shape, with a woman who wouldn't settle for the estate.

When the Upanishad tells the story a second time, it calls Maitreyi a brahmavadini, one who discusses Brahman. Her question is still the one this road asks: what, out of everything I could have, will actually last?

how: In Vedanta study, the dialogue of Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi is a core text, and its line about seeing, hearing, reflecting and meditating is taught as the threefold method of shravana, manana and nididhyasana.

o: action, even asking the right question
the wealth you earn by your own work
a duty to stay at home with family

p: no hope of immortality through it

s: the Upanishad says loving people for the sake of the Self is selfish
teachers read it the other way: it points past the ego to the Self, the atman, that does the loving.
Yajnavalkya admits wealth won't make her immortal
your life would be like the life of the rich, he says; no hope of immortality through wealth.
in the Upanishad's second telling, Maitreyi is called a brahmavadini
one who discusses Brahman: the text remembers her as a thinker in her own right.

games.q: you're Maitreyi. your husband is leaving to become a renunciant and offers you half of everything he owns. what do you say?
o: would the whole earth's wealth make me immortal? tell me what you know.
games.why: she asks what wealth can't give. delighted, Yajnavalkya teaches her about the Self, and the jnana road has quoted her ever since.

practice: Let the people and things most dear to you come to mind, one at a time, and ask Yajnavalkya's question: what is it in me that holds them dear?
Don't look for an answer in words; look for the one who loves, and if you find nothing to hold on to, just rest in the looking. If you pray, you can make Maitreyi's question your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and Maitreyi's action was a question: tell me what you know. On the jnana road, asking is the first step.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Self, the innermost being; Brihadaranyaka 2.4 says all things are dear for its sake.

carryVoice: Take this with you: atman. All we love, we love for the sake of the Self. Maitreyi asked, and the Upanishad kept her question. Day three hundred seven.

sources.q: ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.1–2.4.5 (Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi); retold again at 4.5
